title: The boundary layer: the thin slow skin of flow next to a surface
examples: How thick is a boundary layer?
Why does a golf ball have dimples?

curves.label: Laminar layer
curves.ask: How thick is a boundary layer?

explain.say: In 1904 Ludwig Prandtl solved a puzzle that had stuck fluid mechanics for a century. Viscosity seemed tiny for air, yet drag was real. His answer: all the action happens in a very thin layer next to the surface, the boundary layer. Look at the layers: full speed above, zero at the wall.

explain.say: Inside this layer viscosity matters, because the speed changes from zero to full in a tiny distance. Outside it, you can treat air as frictionless and use Bernoulli. The layer is defined to end where the speed reaches 99 percent of the stream. Which part of the layer causes the friction drag?

draw.text: Edge of the layer: speed reaches 99 % of the free stream

explain.say: The part right at the wall, where the speed changes fastest. Now the graph. Air at 10 metres per second flows along a flat plate. The layer grows with distance, as the square root of x. For a laminar layer, delta equals 5 x over root Re x. At half a metre, Re x is 333,000 and delta is just 4.3 millimetres.

curves.ask: How thick is a boundary layer?

explain.say: At about Re x of half a million, here near 0.75 metres, the layer turns turbulent. A turbulent layer mixes fast air down to the wall, so it can cling to a curved surface longer before it separates, peels away and leaves a wake. That leads to a famous trick. Can you guess it?

explain.say: Golf ball dimples! They make the layer turbulent, so it separates further back, the wake shrinks and drag roughly halves. Wonderful job. Exam tip: a turbulent layer has more skin friction but delays separation, which on blunt bodies cuts the bigger pressure drag.

faq.a: The thin region next to a surface where viscosity slows the fluid from the free-stream speed to zero at the wall. Outside it the flow behaves as if it had no viscosity.

faq.q: How thick is a boundary layer?
faq.a: For a laminar layer on a flat plate, thickness is about 5 x divided by the square root of the local Reynolds number. For air at 10 metres per second, half a metre along, that is about 4.3 millimetres.

faq.q: When does a boundary layer become turbulent?
faq.a: On a smooth flat plate, transition usually happens at a local Reynolds number of about five hundred thousand.

faq.q: Why does a golf ball have dimples?
faq.a: The dimples make the boundary layer turbulent. A turbulent layer clings to the ball longer, so the wake behind is smaller and the drag is much lower.
When the boundary layer cannot keep moving against rising pressure on the back of a body, it stops and peels off the surface, leaving a wide wake of eddies and high drag.

facts: Ludwig Prandtl introduced the boundary layer concept in 1904.
On a smooth flat plate, transition to turbulence usually occurs near Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵.

quiz.say: A laminar boundary layer is 2 millimetres thick at 0.1 metres from the leading edge. Roughly how thick is it at 0.4 metres?
quiz.show: A laminar layer is 2 mm thick at x = 0.1 m. Thickness at x = 0.4 m?
quiz.why: δ grows with √x; x is four times bigger, so δ is √4 = 2 times bigger: 4 mm.

wrong.1: That assumes δ grows in proportion to x, but it grows with the square root.
wrong.2: The layer keeps growing along the plate.

quiz.say: Why can a turbulent boundary layer reduce the drag of a sphere?
quiz.show: How can a turbulent boundary layer reduce drag on a sphere?

options.show: It separates later, so the wake is smaller
options.say: It separates later, so the wake is smaller

options.show: It makes the air less dense
options.say: It makes the air less dense

quiz.why: Turbulent mixing feeds energy to the wall, delaying separation and shrinking the high-drag wake.

wrong.1: Turbulent layers actually have more skin friction; the gain is in pressure drag.
wrong.2: Density is not changed by the boundary layer.
